## Why we version our work

Every analysis reaches the point where someone asks a question the files
alone cannot answer. Which version produced the number in the deck? What
did we change after the review? Can we get back to Friday's model without
undoing Monday's fix?

Git answers those questions by recording your project as a series of
snapshots you choose to keep. Each snapshot carries a message explaining
why you made it. That history is what turns a folder of files into work
you can hand to a colleague, revisit in a year, or safely experiment on.

This lesson covers the loop you will use every day: save a version, look
at the history, branch off to try something, and bring it back. We work in
R and Python examples here, but Git does not care what is in your files —
the same commands cover notebooks, Quarto documents, SQL, and Dockerfiles.

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
### About the exercises

Each exercise below is a real Git repository running inside this page.
Nothing is installed, nothing is uploaded, and nothing touches your
computer — when you reload or press **Reset**, the repository goes away.

Type commands at the prompt and press Enter. The panel on the right shows
where your files currently live and what your history looks like, so you
can watch each command take effect. Type `help` to see what the sandbox
supports, and use the up arrow to repeat a previous command.
:::

## Saving your first version

Three commands do almost all of the work.

`git init` tells Git to start tracking a folder. It creates a hidden
`.git` directory that holds the history; your own files are untouched.

`git add` chooses what goes into the next snapshot. This step surprises
people at first — why not just save everything? Because a working session
usually mixes several things: the fix you want to record, a debugging
print statement you do not, and a data file you should never commit. `git
add` is where you draw that line.

`git commit` writes the snapshot, with a message. A good message finishes
the sentence "this commit will…" — *add the regional breakdown*, *fix the
date parsing in the loader*.

Between them, `git status` tells you where you stand. Run it often; it is
the cheapest command in Git and it always tells you what to do next.

```git-sandbox
id: first-commit
title: Exercise 1 — your first commit
prompt: "~/sales-analysis $"
intro: |
  You have an empty project folder. Nothing is tracked yet.
  Type {y}help{/} to see the available commands.
hints: [git init, git status, 'echo "# Sales analysis" > README.md', git add README.md, 'git commit -m "Add the project README"', git log --oneline]
done-note: Edit, stage, commit — you will repeat that loop for the rest of your career.
tasks:
  - text: Start tracking this folder with `git init`
    when: repo
  - text: 'Create a file, for example `echo "# Sales analysis" > README.md`'
    when: file README.md
  - text: Check where you stand with `git status`
    when: ran /^\s*git\s+status/
  - text: Stage the file with `git add`
    when: staged or commits >= 1
  - text: Record it with `git commit -m "your message"`
    when: commits >= 1
  - text: Change the file and commit a second version
    when: commits >= 2
```

## The three places your work lives

The diagram in the exercise is not decoration — it is the mental model
that makes Git click.

Your **working directory** is the folder you actually edit. Git watches it
but does not record anything on its own.

The **staging area** is the snapshot you are assembling. `git add` copies
the current contents of a file into it. This is why editing a file *after*
you stage it leaves that file in both columns: Git is holding the version
you staged, and separately noticing that the file on disk has moved on.

The **repository** is the permanent history. `git commit` takes whatever
is in the staging area and writes it there under a new commit ID. Once
work is committed, it is very hard to lose.

Two commands read that history back to you. `git log --oneline` lists
commits newest first, and `git diff` shows what has changed in your
working directory since the last commit — worth running before every
commit, as a last look at what you are about to record.

## Trying something without breaking anything

So far the history is a straight line. Branches let it fork.

A branch is a movable label pointing at a commit. Creating one costs
nothing and copies nothing; `git checkout -b report` simply makes a new
label at your current commit and points `HEAD` — your current position —
at it. Commits you make now extend the branch and leave `main` exactly
where it was.

This is what makes Git worth learning. You can restructure a model, try a
different chart library, or rewrite a section of a report, and if it does
not work out you switch back to `main` and the experiment simply is not
part of the story. When you switch branches, Git rewrites the files in
your working directory to match — so the folder always reflects the branch
you are on.

```git-sandbox
id: branching
title: Exercise 2 — work on a branch
prompt: "~/sales-analysis $"
intro: |
  This project already has some history. Run {y}git log --oneline{/} to see it.
  Your job: draft a report on a branch, then bring it back to {y}main{/}.
hints: [git log --oneline, git checkout -b report, git branch, 'echo "# Q3 findings" > report.qmd', git add ., 'git commit -m "Draft the Q3 report"', git checkout main, git merge report]
done-note: Because main had not moved, Git just slid the label forward. That is a fast-forward merge.
seed: |
  git init
  echo "# Sales analysis" > README.md
  git add .
  git commit -m "Add the project README"
  echo "library(tidyverse)" > analysis.R
  git add .
  git commit -m "Start the analysis script"
tasks:
  - text: Create a branch called `report` and switch to it, with `git checkout -b report`
    when: branch report
  - text: Make at least one commit on `report`
    when: commits on report >= 3
  - text: Switch back to `main` and notice your new file is gone from `ls`
    when: ran /^\s*git\s+(checkout|switch)\s+main\s*$/
  - text: Bring the work across with `git merge report`
    when: on main and merged report into main
```

## Bringing work back together

`git merge` combines two lines of work. What it does depends on whether
the branch you are merging into has moved.

If `main` has not moved since you branched, there is nothing to reconcile.
Git just slides the `main` label forward to your branch's commit. That is
a **fast-forward**, and it is what you saw above — the history stays a
straight line.

If `main` *has* moved — a colleague merged something, or you pushed a
hotfix — the two branches have genuinely diverged. Git combines both sets
of changes and records a **merge commit**, the one commit in your history
with two parents. In the graph it is the point where two lanes come back
together, and it is a useful marker: it tells you exactly when a piece of
work joined the mainline.

Git merges different files, and different regions of the same file,
without help. It asks you to intervene only when two branches changed the
same lines — a merge conflict. Conflicts are normal, not a sign you did
something wrong, and they are the subject of the next lesson.

```git-sandbox
id: merging
title: Exercise 3 — a real merge
prompt: "~/sales-analysis $"
intro: |
  A colleague has been working on the {y}forecast{/} branch while you fix things on {y}main{/}.
  Run {y}git log --oneline{/} on each branch, then merge them and watch the graph.
hints: [git branch, git log --oneline, 'echo "fixed" > hotfix.md', git add ., 'git commit -m "Fix the date parsing"', git merge forecast, git branch -d forecast]
done-note: Two lanes, one merge commit. That shape is the whole story of how the work came together.
seed: |
  git init
  echo "# Sales analysis" > README.md
  git add .
  git commit -m "Add the project README"
  git checkout -b forecast
  echo "arima(sales)" > forecast.R
  git add .
  git commit -m "Add a first forecast model"
  echo "tune the model" >> forecast.R
  git add .
  git commit -m "Tune the forecast parameters"
  git checkout main
tasks:
  - text: Commit a change on `main` so the two branches diverge
    when: commits on main >= 2 and not merged main into forecast
  - text: Merge `forecast` into `main`
    when: on main and merged forecast into main
  - text: Confirm the history now contains a merge commit with two parents
    when: merge commit
  - text: 'Tidy up: delete the merged branch with `git branch -d forecast`'
    when: not branch forecast and ran /git\s+branch\s+-[dD]/
```

## Command reference

| Command | What it does |
|---|---|
| `git init` | Start tracking the current folder |
| `git status` | Show what has changed and what is staged |
| `git add <file>` | Stage a file for the next commit |
| `git add .` | Stage every change in the folder |
| `git commit -m "…"` | Record the staged changes as a new commit |
| `git log --oneline` | List the history, newest first |
| `git diff` | Show unstaged changes since the last commit |
| `git branch` | List branches; `git branch <name>` creates one |
| `git checkout -b <name>` | Create a branch and switch to it |
| `git checkout <name>` | Switch to an existing branch |
| `git merge <name>` | Merge a branch into the current one |
| `git branch -d <name>` | Delete a branch you have already merged |

: {tbl-colwidths="[36,64]"}

## Where to go next

Everything so far happens on one machine. The next lesson adds a remote —
a shared copy on GitHub, GitLab, or an internal server — and the two
commands that keep it in step, `git push` and `git pull`. That is the
point where version control becomes collaboration, and where pull requests
and code review fit in.

Three habits are worth starting now:

**Commit small and often.** A commit that changes one thing is a commit
you can understand, revert, or explain a year from now.

**Write messages for the next reader.** That reader is usually you.

**Keep data and secrets out of the repository.** A `.gitignore` file
tells Git what to leave alone — credentials, large data files, rendered
output. Getting this right at the start of a project saves considerable
trouble later.

Finally, you do not have to work at the command line. The Git pane in
RStudio and the Source Control view in Positron run these same commands
behind buttons, and the concepts you learned here — staging, committing,
branching, merging — are exactly what those buttons do. Learning the
commands first means the interface makes sense rather than the other way
round.
